overview: A two-page register of papers filed under the subject of immigration into the Kwantung Leased Territory, summarizing twenty-one reports sent chiefly from Dairen between 1933 and 1937. Most entries concern quarterly statistics on Chinese laborer arrivals and departures through Dairen, with occasional comparative figures for Newchwang, while several address immigration quotas, entry restrictions, permit refusals, and regulations governing the temporary admission and residence of foreign workers. The register identifies reporting officers and indicates that detailed correspondence was generally sent to the U.S. Embassy in Tokyo.

subfiles.title: List of papers on immigration into the Kwantung Leased Territory
subfiles.about: A register summarizes twenty-one consular reports concerning Chinese immigration, emigration, labor controls, and alien employment in the Kwantung Leased Territory from 1933 through 1937.
subfiles.summary: The register principally records quarterly statistical reports on Chinese laborers arriving at and departing from Dairen, sometimes including comparative data for Newchwang. Other entries cover an annual immigration quota of 440,000, the refusal of an entry certificate by the Tsingtao office of the Ta Tung Company, and Ordinance No. 15 of March 20, 1918, governing the temporary admission and residence of aliens employed in the Kwantung Leased Territory. The reports were submitted by Vincent, Perkins, Sukokin, and Grummon, usually to the U.S. Embassy in Tokyo. A closing note directs researchers to catalogue cards for later correspondence.

interest: The register provides a compact chronological map of a longer consular reporting series and shows how closely American officials monitored Chinese labor movements through Japanese-controlled Dairen. Particularly useful are its references to otherwise dispersed statistical tables, the 440,000-person quota, the regulatory authority exercised by the Ta Tung Company, and a translated 1918 ordinance governing foreign workers. It also reveals gaps in official knowledge—notably difficulties obtaining figures from ports elsewhere in Manchuria—and directs historians to subsequent correspondence filed through catalogue cards.
